fields.value: Video annotation of head-gaze direction; headset microphones and Julius adintool for speech intervals; Kinect face tracking for face position and rotation; Microcone for audio-source direction; Kinect skeleton data for target head position. No participant questionnaires or interviews are described.

quotes.text: Video sequences capturing for the overall picture of all of their interactions were recorded, and the directions of their head gaze (who was looking at whom) were annotated using a video annotation tool, ELAN.
Each participant’s speech was recorded using headset microphones, and their speech intervals were detected using the Julius speech recognition adintool software.
In addition, a Microsoft Kinect sensor was set in front of each participant, and the participant’s face position and rotation were measured using Kinect’s face tracking function.
The audio-source angle is obtained using a microcone1 that can recognize six different directions through a microphone array.

fields.value: The observational analysis found that higher-dominance participants switched gaze more often. For a less-dominant side participant, gaze remained on the speaker 71% of the time (average duration 1.27 s); for a dominant side participant, this was 52%. No statistical significance tests are reported. The addressee head-direction estimator achieved about 80% accuracy.

quotes.text: For example, when a side participant was less dominant, they looked continuously at the speaker 71% of the time (gaze duration of 1.27 s), and changed their gaze toward the addressee 15% of the time.
when a side participant was dominant, they looked continuously at the speaker 52% of the time, and switched their gaze to the addressee or another side participant more frequently.
With an accuracy of about 80% using a leave-one-person-out evaluation, the model is sufficient for estimating a speaker’s head direction automatically.

fields.value: The paper frames robot head gaze as attentional behavior needed for participation in multiparty conversation, shaped by participation roles and dominance.

quotes.text: A robot’s gaze behaviors are indispensable in allowing the robot to participate in multiparty conversations.

To build a robot that can convey appropriate attentional behavior in multiparty human- robot conversations, this study proposes robot head gaze models in terms of participation roles and dominance in a conversation.

fields.value: Gaze communicates attention appropriate to a participant's conversational role; speakers mainly look at the addressee, while side participants look toward the speaker, addressee, or other side participants. Dominance also affects gaze allocation and switching.

quotes.text: A speaker looks at an addressee for the majority of their speaking time, occasionally paying attention to any existing side participants.
The side participants, on the other hand, tend to look at either the speaker or the addressee.

Therefore, a communication robot as a participant in multiparty interactions with human users is required to be able to generate appropriate gaze and attentional behavior that corresponds to the robot’s role at any given time.
Therefore, dominance in a conversation affects the participant’s gaze behaviors.

fields.value: In human conversation observations, higher-dominance participants switched gaze more frequently. Effects of robot gaze on people or interaction were not evaluated in this paper.

quotes.text: These results suggest that participants with higher dominance have a greater chance to switch their gaze.
As future work, we plan to evaluate the system by conducting a user study

fields.value: The system estimates speaker and addressee roles using Microcone audio direction and Kinect head-direction recognition, identifies side participants as those who are neither speaker nor addressee, estimates dominance with a regression model, and chooses gaze transitions and durations from role- and dominance-specific models. The robot turns its head toward Kinect-tracked target positions.

quotes.text: The system identifies the speaker based on the audio-source angle.
Hence, the system identifies the addressee by recognizing the target for the speaker’s gaze when the speaker begins talking.
After determining the current speaker and corresponding addressee, the persons who are neither the speaker nor the addressee are identified as side participants.
Once the participation roles and dominance are estimated, the gaze of the robot is determined by referring to the gaze-transition models proposed in Section 2.

fields.value: Robovie R3 humanoid robot; gaze is controlled by rotating its head.

quotes.text: We used a Robovie R3 to implement the robot gaze.
To control the head direction of the robot, the system measures the angle between its current head direction and the direction of its next target.

fields.value: The authors analyzed gaze in four-person free conversations and modeled head-gaze transitions by conversational role and dominance. They implemented those models on a Robovie R3, but did not evaluate the robot with users; their human data suggested that more dominant participants switched gaze more often.

RQ1 — The paper frames robot gaze as attentional behavior for multiparty participation but does not give a formal definition. RQ2 — It describes gaze functions across speaker, addressee, and side-participant roles. RQ3 — It reports observed gaze differences associated with dominance, not effects of robot gaze on people. RQ4 — It details sensing, role and dominance estimation, gaze models, and head control. RQ5 — It identifies the humanoid Robovie R3. RQ6 — It does not discuss how embodiment influenced the study.
